Air quality

Source: vignettes/air-quality.Rmd
air-quality.Rmd

The Air Quality tab of the golemenviro app compares the particles with the air quality guidelines of the World Health Organization (2021). The guidelines are for the averages of whole days and years, not for single readings. In R, get_daily() downloads the averages of the days, who_guidelines holds the guidelines, and plot_daily_means() draws the days against them. Gauges and time series shows how to install the package and which servers it reads.

library(golemenviro)
Sys.setenv(TZ = "Europe/Bucharest")
url <- "http://pip1.crabdance.com:1507/api/v1/query_range"

The days run from midnight to midnight in the time zone of the R session, here the one of the app, as Gauges and time series explains.

The guidelines 

who_guidelines
#>   metric day year
#> 1   PM25  15    5
#> 2   PM10  45   15

day is the guideline for the average of a day, which should not be exceeded on more than 3 to 4 days a year, and year the one for the average of a year, both in µg/m³. PM1 has none.

Download the daily averages

get_daily() downloads the average of each whole day of one sensor, over the days days before today, 30 by default. Like get_hourly(), it takes the name of the sensor in Prometheus, "PM25" for PM2.5. Today, still running, is left out, and so is a day with readings in fewer than 18 of its hours, as in the usual rules for daily averages of air quality:

pm25 <- get_daily(url, "PM25", days = 30)
tail(pm25)
#>          date    value hours
#> 25 2026-11-13 18.46389    24
#> 26 2026-11-14 19.09444    24
#> 27 2026-11-15 16.05972    24
#> 28 2026-11-16 17.94028    24
#> 29 2026-11-17 19.78750    24
#> 30 2026-11-18 11.55347    24

It has a row per day: its date, the average value, and how many hours had readings. When the server cannot be reached, get_daily() returns NULL with a message.

Days against the guideline

plot_daily_means() draws the days of a particle sensor as bars, with the guideline for a day as a dashed line, so that the days above it stand out. variable names the sensor in the title and the hover labels, and guideline sets the line. The axis starts at 0 and always reaches above the guideline:

guideline <- who_guidelines$day[who_guidelines$metric == "PM25"]
plot_daily_means(pm25, "PM2.5", guideline)

The app counts the days above the guideline, and sets the average of the period against the guideline for a year:

sum(pm25$value > guideline)
#> [1] 18
round(mean(pm25$value), 1)
#> [1] 19.3

The guideline for a year is for the average of a whole year, so for a shorter period it is only a pointer.

A year of PM10

For a longer period, raise days:

pm10 <- get_daily(url, "PM10", days = 365)
guideline_pm10 <- who_guidelines$day[who_guidelines$metric == "PM10"]
plot_daily_means(pm10, "PM10", guideline_pm10)

The guideline allows 3 to 4 days above it in a year. To count them over this year:

sum(pm10$value > guideline_pm10)
#> [1] 34

Dark mode and saving

Like the charts of Daily pattern and comfort, plot_daily_means() takes mode = "dark", which makes the bars and the dashed line lighter for a dark page. It leaves the background white, so the code is not run here:

plot_daily_means(pm25, "PM2.5", guideline, mode = "dark")

The charts are plotly objects, so htmlwidgets::saveWidget() saves any of them as a web page:

chart <- plot_daily_means(pm25, "PM2.5", guideline)
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(chart, "pm25.html")
